title: Demonstrate an understanding of healthy farm animals

lessons.title: How to tell if an animal is healthy
lessons.html:
Look at your animals every day

Cattle, sheep, goats, pigs and chickens cannot tell you when they are sick. You must learn to see it. The best time to look is when you count them in the morning, when they are fed or when they come to the water trough or kraal.

Signs of a healthy animal

  • Alert: head up, ears moving, eyes bright and clear.
  • Moves well: walks easily with the herd, no limping.
  • Eats and drinks normally; cattle, sheep and goats chew the cud when resting.
  • Coat or wool is smooth and shiny, not rough or falling out.
  • Breathing is calm and even when resting.
  • Dung is normal for that animal: firm, not watery, no blood.
  • Body condition is good: not too thin, ribs and hip bones not sticking out.

Signs of a sick animal

  • Stands alone, away from the herd, head low.
  • Does not eat or drink, or stops chewing the cud.
  • Fast or difficult breathing, coughing.
  • Runny nose or eyes, drooling, sores on the mouth or feet.
  • Diarrhoea, blood in dung or urine.
  • Limping, swollen joints or swelling under the jaw.
  • A swollen, tight belly (bloat) on the left side in cattle and sheep.
  • Pale gums or inner eyelids in sheep and goats, which can mean worms.

What to do

If you see a sick animal, report it to your supervisor at once. Write down the animal's number or ear tag, what you saw and when. If possible, separate it gently from the others in a sick pen. Do not treat it yourself unless you have been trained and told to.

lessons.title: Keeping animals healthy
lessons.html:
Prevention is better than cure

It costs much less to keep animals healthy than to treat sick ones. Good care has five parts.

1. Food and water

Animals need enough good grazing or feed and clean, fresh water every day. Check troughs and drinkers daily. Clean them and fix leaks. In winter when the veld is dry, the farm may give extra feed or licks.

2. Shelter and space

Animals need shade in summer and shelter from cold wind and rain. Kraals and pens must be clean and dry, with no sharp wire or nails that can cut them. Do not overcrowd.

3. Disease control

  • Vaccinations protect against diseases. The farm and vet set the programme.
  • Dipping or pour-ons control ticks, which spread diseases such as redwater and heartwater.
  • Dosing controls worms in sheep and goats.
  • Keep new or sick animals apart before mixing them with the herd.
  • Follow the product label and your vet for all medicines. Write down every treatment.

4. Handling with care

Handle animals quietly. Do not shout, hit or use sharp sticks. The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 makes cruelty to animals a crime. Calm animals are also safer for you.

5. Reporting notifiable diseases

Some diseases, such as foot-and-mouth disease, are controlled by the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984 and must be reported to the state vet. If you see blisters on mouths or feet, many animals sick at once, or sudden deaths, tell your supervisor immediately.

Safety for you

Some animal diseases can spread to people. Wear gloves when handling sick or dead animals, afterbirths or aborted foetuses. Wash your hands well with soap. Never eat meat from an animal that died of unknown causes.

Key points

  • A healthy animal is alert, eats well and moves normally.
  • A sick animal often stands alone, stops eating or breathes fast.
  • Report sick animals to your supervisor at once and record what you saw.
  • Good feed, clean water, shelter and a disease programme keep animals healthy.
  • Wear gloves with sick or dead animals and wash your hands.

Alert, with bright eyes and chewing the cud
